items.stimulus: Economists have long debated whether loyalty to a single employer pays off over the course of a career. One study of payroll records followed nearly 30,000 employees across a decade and tracked every change of firm. Compared with peers who remained at a single firm for the full period, ______

the wages of employees who changed firms at least twice grew about 9 percent faster.

items.explanation: The phrase 'Compared with peers who remained at a single firm' must be followed by people who can be compared with those peers. Choice A begins with 'employees who changed firms', so the comparison is between two groups of workers.

the eruption that buried the forest left each tree where it had grown.

items.stimulus: Much of the water in a deep aquifer began as rain that fell on the land above it. Groundwater moves far more slowly than water in rivers, often only a few meters a year. Seeping downward through layers of sand, gravel, and fractured rock, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: hydrologists find that rainwater takes several decades to arrive.
the journey of rainwater can last for several decades.
rainwater can take several decades to reach the aquifer.
the sand and gravel slowly filter rainwater for decades.
items.explanation: The opening phrase 'Seeping downward through layers of sand, gravel, and fractured rock' has no subject of its own. That means the first noun after the comma has to be the thing doing the seeping. The thing that seeps through rock is the rainwater, so the choice that starts with 'rainwater' is the only one where the phrase attaches correctly. This is the one check behind every dangling-modifier question on the test: name who did the action in the opening phrase, then find the choice that puts that noun first. Once you can do it here, you can do it in the longer Medium and Hard versions, where all four choices sound fluent.

A.why: You picked the people who study the water instead of the water itself. Placed right after the comma, 'hydrologists' becomes the subject, so the sentence says the scientists are seeping through the rock. The word 'rainwater' appears later in the choice, but only the first noun decides what the opening phrase describes.

B.why: This is the 'the X of...' trap. The subject here is 'the journey', and a journey can't seep through gravel. 'Rainwater' sits inside the phrase 'of rainwater', so it isn't the subject. You let the related word fool you into thinking the right noun came first.

D.why: You put first the material the water passes through, not the thing that is moving. In the opening phrase, the sand and gravel are what something seeps through, so they can't be what's doing the seeping. This choice reverses the roles the passage sets up, even though 'sand and gravel' repeats words from the phrase and sounds like a natural fit.

items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: the fossil leaves still displaying their branching veins and tiny breathing pores.
paleobotanists can still see the leaves' branching veins and tiny breathing pores.
the leaves' branching veins and tiny breathing pores are still clearly visible.
the fossil leaves still display their branching veins and tiny breathing pores.
items.explanation: The fossil leaves are what was 'preserved in fine volcanic ash for roughly 50 million years'. Choice D puts 'the fossil leaves' directly after the comma and gives them the finite verb 'display', so the modifier attaches correctly and the sentence is complete.

A.why: You chose the right first noun, but 'displaying' is an -ing form and not a conjugated verb. 'The fossil leaves' never gets a main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

B.why: You put the scientists first. Paleobotanists weren't preserved in volcanic ash for 50 million years. This is the trap of naming the people who work with the object instead of the object itself.

C.why: You picked a property of the leaves instead of the leaves. The subject here is 'veins and... pores', with 'leaves'' reduced to a possessive. That is the object-instead-of-its-property trap, and it leaves the opening phrase describing the wrong thing.

items.stimulus: Each spring, collisions between warm Gulf air and cold continental air make the Great Plains one of the world's most active regions for severe weather. Towering as high as fifteen kilometers above the plains, ______ hail, lightning, and damaging winds within an hour of first appearing on radar.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: a cumulonimbus cloud, fed by updrafts that can exceed 100 kilometers per hour, often produce
the updrafts feeding a cumulonimbus cloud, which can exceed 100 kilometers per hour, often produce
a cumulonimbus cloud, fed by updrafts that can exceed 100 kilometers per hour, often produces
a cumulonimbus cloud is fed by updrafts that can exceed 100 kilometers per hour, it often produces
items.explanation: Start by asking what is 'towering as high as fifteen kilometers above the plains.' It is the cloud, so the first noun after the comma has to be 'a cumulonimbus cloud.' Three choices pass that test, so finding the right subject is not enough. Next, check what follows it. The phrase 'fed by updrafts that can exceed 100 kilometers per hour' is an interrupter. If you cross it out, you get 'a cumulonimbus cloud... often produces.' A singular subject takes the singular verb 'produces.' The sentence also needs exactly one main clause, and this choice gives it one. Only C meets all three conditions: the right subject, a verb that agrees with it, and a sound sentence boundary.

A.why: You found the right subject, then let the plural nouns in the interrupter ('updrafts,' 'kilometers') set the verb. The subject is still the singular 'cloud,' so 'produce' doesn't agree with it. It needs 'produces.'

B.why: You chose a noun closely related to the cloud instead of the cloud itself. Updrafts are rising air inside the cloud, and they don't 'tower' fifteen kilometers above the plains. Because 'the updrafts' comes first after the comma, the opening phrase is left dangling.

D.why: The opening noun is right, but this choice joins two independent clauses ('a cumulonimbus cloud is fed...' and 'it often produces...') with only a comma. That's a comma splice. Getting the subject right doesn't make up for a broken sentence boundary.

the ferryman tale, documented by collectors in at least six countries, survive
the ferryman tale was documented by collectors in at least six countries, it survives

D.why: This choice starts with the right noun but creates two independent clauses, 'the ferryman tale was documented...' and 'it survives...', joined only by a comma. That's a comma splice, so the sentence fails even though the modifier attaches correctly.

items.stimulus: Linguists who study whistled languages have long asked how much of a spoken tongue a whistle can carry. On La Gomera, in the Canary Islands, herders still use Silbo Gomero, a whistled form of Spanish. Stripped of most vowel distinctions and reduced to rising and falling pitches, ______ across ravines more than two kilometers wide.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: the herders' messages, which listeners decode by context, carry
the herders, whose listeners decode the messages by context, send them
the messages of the herders, decoded by listeners from context, carries
listeners decode the herders' messages by context as they travel
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something that has been stripped of vowel distinctions and reduced to pitches. Only the messages fit. In choice A, 'herders'' is a possessive that modifies the head noun 'messages', so the subject is 'messages'. That plural subject correctly takes 'carry', and the relative clause has its own finite verb, 'decode'.

B.why: You put the people who make the messages in the subject position. That says the herders themselves were stripped of vowels and reduced to pitches. This is the maker-for-the-thing trap.

C.why: You found the right subject, 'messages', but then matched the verb to the nearby singular noun 'context'. 'Messages' is plural and needs 'carry', not 'carries'.

D.why: You chose the people affected rather than the thing described. That makes the listeners the ones stripped of vowels and reduced to pitches.

items.stimulus: In a four-year trial in Iowa, agronomists compared fields planted with a winter cover of cereal rye against fields left bare between harvests. Rooted deeply enough to reach nitrate that would otherwise leach into groundwater, ______ the following spring.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: the rye, once tilled under, returning much of that nitrogen to the soil
the rye returned much of that nitrogen to the soil once it was tilled under
the agronomists found that the rye returned much of that nitrogen to the soil
the rye's nitrogen was returned to the soil once the plants were tilled under
items.explanation: Only a plant can be 'rooted deeply enough to reach nitrate', so the rye has to come right after the comma. Choice B starts with 'the rye' and gives it a finite main verb, 'returned', which makes the sentence complete.

A.why: You put the right noun first, but 'returning' is an -ing form and can't be a main verb. The sentence never gets a finite verb, so it's a fragment.

C.why: You let the researchers take the subject position. That says the agronomists were rooted in the soil. This is the trap of putting the people acting in the study in place of the plant.

D.why: 'Rye's' is only a possessive. The subject is 'nitrogen', a substance the rye took up, and nitrogen isn't rooted in anything. This is the trap of putting the object's property in place of the object.
